script.text: Microfluidic chips move tiny volumes of fluid through channels that are narrower than a human hair.
Efficient mixing is difficult in such channels because the flow is laminar and diffusion is slow.
Engineers therefore add herringbone grooves or serpentine sections that fold the fluid onto itself.
The resulting flow field is complicated, and characterization usually requires fluorescence microscopy.

We found that a fixed threshold suffices for most clips, but flickering illumination needs an adaptive threshold.
Trajectory linking is the most fragile step, since particles leave the focal plane and reappear later.
Our linker tolerates gaps of up to three frames and rejects links that imply unphysical accelerations.

selection.text: The largest diﬀerences appear close to the channel
walls, where few particles are observed. Increasing
the particle density reduces this eﬀect but also incr-
eases the number of ambiguous links. A practical
compromise is a density of roughly one particle per
ﬁfty square micrometres. Finally, all intermediate
ﬁles are stored so that every reconstruction can be
audited and reproduced.

A practical compromise is a density of roughly one particle per fifty square micrometres.
Finally, all intermediate files are stored so that every reconstruction can be audited and reproduced.

selection.text: We tested the workﬂow on three chip designs with
diﬀerent groove conﬁgurations. Each design was
ﬁlmed at ﬁve ﬂow rates, giving ﬁfteen clips of
twenty seconds each. Processing one clip takes
about four minutes on an ordinary oﬃce laptop. The
diﬀerential pressure across the chip was recorded
independently as a consistency check.

script.text: We tested the workflow on three chip designs with different groove configurations.
Each design was filmed at five flow rates, giving fifteen clips of twenty seconds each.
Processing one clip takes about four minutes on an ordinary office laptop.
The differential pressure across the chip was recorded independently as a consistency check.

selection.text: The herringbone design produced the most complic-
ated ﬁeld and the largest reconstruction error. Its
staggered grooves create counter-rotating vortices
that particles cross only brieﬂy. Nevertheless, the
main recirculation zones were identiﬁed correctly in
every clip. We conclude that oﬄine reconstruction is
suﬃcient for routine quality control of fabricated
chips.

script.text: The herringbone design produced the most complicated field and the largest reconstruction error.
Its staggered grooves create counter-rotating vortices that particles cross only briefly.
Nevertheless, the main recirculation zones were identified correctly in every clip.
We conclude that offline reconstruction is sufficient for routine quality control of fabricated chips.
